# Part A - Creating Data Frames
```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
name
age
passed
```
```{r}
students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
students
```
```{r}
typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)
```
```{r}
courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)
courses
```

## Question #1
Since a data frame is a table, every column must have the same number of rows; otherwise, some cells would be blank. If the lengths do not match, R shows an error like "arguments imply differing number of rows: 3, 2".

## Question #2
A data frame is a list where each element is a column, and a list can store different types, so columns can differ in type. Each column, however, is a vector, and vectors can store only one type. So all the values in the same column must be the same type.

# Part B - Subsetting Data Frames
```{r}
students$age
students[["age"]]
students["age"]
```
```{r}
students[2, ]
```
```{r}
students[3, "name"]
```
```{r}
students[students$passed == TRUE, ]
```
```{r}
students[students$passed == TRUE & students$age > 19, ]
```

## Question #3
```{r}
class(students$age)
class(students[["age"]])
class(students["age"])
```
`students$age` and `students[["age"]]` both give `"numeric"`, the plain vector of ages. `students["age"]` gives a `"data.frame"`, because single brackets keep the structure and return a smaller table. It works like lists, where `[ ]` returns a list and `[[ ]]` returns the element itself.

## Question #4
The `&` operator compares the two logical vectors position by position, giving TRUE only for students who meet both conditions. R keeps just the rows marked TRUE. With `|`, a student who meets either condition is kept, so the result would have more rows.

```

```

## Question #5
For age (numeric), `summary()` shows the minimum, quartiles, median, mean, and maximum. For passed (logical), it counts the FALSE and TRUE values, and for name (character), it shows the length, class, and mode only. A mean is meaningless for name because you cannot average text.

## Question #6
I would use `str()` first when I load a data frame, because it shows the size, the type of each column, and a sample of the values. I would use `summary()` next to look at the values through statistics like the mean, median, and counts.

# Part D - Data Frame Operations
```{r}
students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)
students
```
```{r}
students$passed <- NULL
students
```
```{r}
students[order(students$age), ]
```
```{r}
students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

## Question #7
```{r}
students[students$passed == TRUE, ]
```

No, the filter no longer works as expected because the `passed` column was deleted. `students$passed` is now NULL, so no rows are returned, and R gives no error. Because each operation changes the data frame, I need to keep track of its current columns so later steps don't quietly fail or give wrong results.

## Question #8
First, `order(students$age)` gives the row numbers arranged from the youngest to the oldest student (for example, 3, 1, 5, 2, 4). Then `students[that vector, ]` selects the rows in that order, and the blank after the comma keeps all the columns. Whole rows move together, so each student's data stays intact.

# Part E - Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
grades
```
```{r}
# The exercise does not give a passing grade, so 75 is assumed here
grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
grades
```
```{r}
grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
```

## Question #9
To analyze the failing students, I'll create a net-change column ('final - midterm') and sort the subset by change and initial midterm grade. This lets us evaluate the root whether poor initial performance or a significant performance drop is more of a trend among those who failed.

# Conclusion
In R, a data frame is a table made of equal-length vectors grouped together, allowing each column to hold a different data type like text or numbers. It is the standard format for tabular data, where every row corresponds to an individual record and every column to a detail about it.
